lessons.title: Man-to-man basics
lessons.objective: Describe man defense, closeouts and denying the pass.

payload.prompt: Each defender is assigned one opponent to follow. Man or zone?

scene.alt: Five defenders each stay close to a different offensive player as the offense moves around the floor.

explanation.correct: In man-to-man, each defender owns a person and follows him around the floor. A zone defender owns an area instead and guards whoever comes into it.
explanation.incorrect: Zone defenders guard an area of the floor and pick up whoever enters it. When every defender follows one assigned opponent, that is man-to-man.

payload.prompt: A defender stands in the passing lane with an arm out, refusing to let his man catch the ball. What is it?

scene.alt: A defender stands between his man and the passer, one arm extended into the passing lane.

explanation.correct: Denying the pass means getting between the ball and your man so he cannot catch it. The offense then has to work harder just to get him a touch.
explanation.incorrect: A closeout is a sprint at a shooter who already has the ball. Standing in the lane with an arm out to keep your man from catching it is denial.

payload.prompt: What is a closeout?

options.text: Sprinting at a shooter who just received a pass, trying to contest without fouling.
Guarding someone in the paint.
Ending the game after the final basket.

explanation.correct: A closeout is a fast run at a shooter who just got the ball, slowing into short steps with a hand up so you contest the shot without flying past or fouling.
explanation.incorrect: A closeout is not guarding the paint or ending a game. It is the sprint-then-stop at a shooter who has caught the ball, meant to contest the shot under control.

payload.prompt: Match each defensive action to what it does.

pairs.definition: Guarding the player with the ball, trying to prevent them from scoring, passing or driving.
Playing tight on your opponent so teammates cannot easily pass them the ball.
Sprinting at a shooter to contest the shot after they receive a pass.

distractorDefinitions: Staying under the basket to block shots.
Pressing full court from baseline to baseline.

explanation.summary: On-ball is primary defense; deny keeps the ball away; closeout contests shots from range.

payload.question: What is she complimenting?

options.text: The defenders guarding the ball handler are tough, tight and hard to get past.
The team only guards the person with the ball.
They are on the ball in the paint.
The team is fouling everyone.

payload.translation: She means the team's defenders are playing great defense on whoever has the ball, making it hard to pass or shoot.

followUps.why: You recognize that good on-ball defense means tight, aggressive play on the ball handler.

followUps.line: Does that help their defense everywhere?
followUps.why: A good follow-up asking whether strong on-ball play helps the whole team.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: On-ball defense is just playing good defense on the person with the ball.

lessons.title: Help defense and rotations
lessons.objective: Read who helps, who rotates and who is left open.

payload.prompt: What is help defense?

options.text: A defender leaving their assigned opponent to stop a drive or penetration by another player.
Passing the ball to a teammate who is open.
A player on the bench coming into the game to substitute.

explanation.correct: Right. Help defense stops penetration by having an extra defender collapse on the ball handler. This leaves someone else open.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Help defense is when a defender leaves their own player to stop a penetrating ball handler, knowing it creates a gap elsewhere.

payload.prompt: What happens when a help defender leaves their player?

options.text: Another defender must rotate over to guard the open player, creating a chain of moves.
The offense stops moving the ball.
That open player automatically scores.

explanation.correct: Exactly. When help defense leaves an opponent, the rotation means another defender slides over to cover that gap. Good rotations stop easy buckets.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. Rotation is the chain of defenders sliding over after help defense creates a gap. Each defender covers someone else in sequence.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: Their help defense is too slow.

payload.question: What is she noticing?

options.text: The defense is not rotating fast enough when help is needed, leaving gaps open.
A player is too slow to run down the court.
The coaching staff is not helping.
They are not scoring fast enough.

payload.translation: She means when defenders try to help on drives, the rotation is sluggish and opposing players get open looks because the movement is delayed.

followUps.line: Yeah, they get beat on penetration.
followUps.why: You recognize that slow help defense leads to easy offensive scoring.
A good follow-up asking whether poor communication is causing the defensive breakdowns.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Help defense needs to be quick and coordinated, or the offense punishes it.

lessons.title: Zone defense and how to beat it
lessons.objective: Describe 2-3, 3-2, 1-3-1 and matchup zones and where the gaps live.

payload.prompt: Match each zone to its formation.

pairs.definition: Two defenders up top, three across the baseline. The most familiar zone, built to protect the paint.
Three defenders across the top, two lower. Built to stay tight on perimeter shooters.
One defender up top, three in the middle, one on the baseline. Often used to trap the wings.

explanation.summary: 2-3 is most common; 3-2 stops shooters; 1-3-1 traps and disrupts.

payload.prompt: Tap the soft spot in the middle of a 2-3 zone.

diagram.alt: Half-court diagram of a 2-3 zone: two defenders above the free-throw line and three along the baseline. The free-throw-line area between them is open.

explanation.correct: The middle of the free-throw line sits between the two top defenders and the three along the baseline, so each group can assume the other has it. A player catching there can shoot, pass or attack.
explanation.incorrect: That spot is guarded by a defender. The soft spot in a 2-3 zone is the middle of the free-throw line, where the top and baseline defenders leave a hole between them.

payload.prompt: How should an offense attack a zone defense?

options.text: Move the ball quickly to find gaps, then shoot open threes or pass into the soft spots.
Dribble alone into the middle against all five defenders.
Stand still and pass slowly around the outside.

explanation.correct: A zone has to shift every time the ball moves. Fast passes stretch it, open threes appear, and a pass into the middle finds a hole.
explanation.incorrect: Zones beat players who dribble into five defenders or pass slowly around the outside. Quick ball movement makes defenders shift and opens gaps.

payload.prompt: What is a matchup zone?

options.text: A hybrid zone where defenders guard an area but also account for nearby opponents, blending zone and man-to-man principles.
Defending players based only on height.
A zone that never changes formation.

explanation.correct: Right. Matchup zones give defenders flexibility: they have a zone to cover but can guard nearby opponents like man-to-man.
explanation.incorrect: Not quite. A matchup zone blends zone principles (guarding an area) with man-to-man principles (accounting for nearby opponents).

lessons.title: Rebounding and the box-out
lessons.objective: Explain boxing out, offensive boards and why rebounds swing games.

payload.prompt: A defender shoves his man's back with two hands to clear space for a rebound. Legal?

scene.alt: Under the basket, a defender pushes an opponent in the back with both hands as a shot comes down.

explanation.correct: A box-out uses your body: turn, make contact with your back and hips, hold your ground and spread your arms. Pushing the opponent with your hands is a foul.
explanation.incorrect: Boxing out is legal when a player turns and uses position and body contact to shield the ball. Shoving with the hands or arms is a pushing foul.

payload.prompt: Why are offensive rebounds valuable?

options.text: They keep the possession alive and give the team another shot.
They count as points for the team that grabs them.
They give the ball to the other team.

explanation.correct: A miss would normally end the possession. An offensive rebound keeps it going, so the team gets another shot at the same basket, and in the NBA the shot clock resets to 14.
explanation.incorrect: An offensive rebound is not a score and it does not hand over the ball. It is the shooting team getting its own miss back, which means another shot.

payload.prompt: What are second-chance points?

options.text: Points scored after an offensive rebound, on the same possession.
Points scored by the team with the second-best record.
Free throws after a missed shot.

explanation.correct: Second-chance points are the points a team scores after grabbing its own miss. They show up in box scores and can swing a close game.
explanation.incorrect: It has nothing to do with records or free throws. Second-chance points come from a possession that continued after an offensive rebound.

payload.prompt: Team A misses. A Team B player grabs the ball. What kind of rebound is it?

scene.alt: After a Team A miss, a Team B player pulls down the rebound.

explanation.correct: Rebounds are named from the rebounder's side. Team B was defending when Team A missed, so grabbing the ball is a defensive rebound and Team B takes possession.
explanation.incorrect: An offensive rebound is the shooting team grabbing its own miss. Here the team that did not shoot got the ball, so it is a defensive rebound.

payload.prompt: A defender watches the shot go up instead of turning to find his man. Boxed out?

scene.alt: A defender stands facing the rim with his eyes on the ball while the opponent he guards slips toward the basket.

explanation.correct: A box-out starts when the shot goes up: turn, find your man, make contact and keep him behind you. A defender who only watches the ball gives up inside position.
explanation.incorrect: Looking at the shot is the classic way to lose a rebound. The defender has to locate his man and get his body between that man and the basket.

payload.prompt: What share of available rebounds does an elite big grab while on the floor?

explanation.correct: Ten players share every miss, so an average player gets about 10%. The best rebounding bigs reach the low-to-mid 20s, which is how much they swing possessions.
explanation.incorrect: With ten players on the floor, an average share is about 10%. Elite rebounding bigs land around the low 20s, more than double that.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: They are killing us on the boards.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: The other team is winning the rebounding battle and getting extra shots.
The other team is fouling a lot.
The other team is shooting a great percentage.
The other team is pressing full court.

payload.translation: The other team is winning the rebounding battle, getting multiple possessions and extra chances to score through offensive boards.

followUps.line: Yeah, they are getting every miss.
followUps.why: You recognize that poor rebounding means the other team gets second chances.

followUps.line: We need to box out better.
followUps.why: A good follow-up identifying the rebounding technique needed to stop it.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need the numbers. 'Are we boxing out?' is a fair question any time your team keeps giving up second shots.

lessons.title: Rim protection and shot contests
lessons.objective: Explain rim protection, verticality and a good contest.

payload.prompt: A defender's hand hits only the ball, cleanly, as it leaves the shooter. Foul?

scene.alt: A leaping defender swats the ball with his hand while it leaves the shooter's fingertips, with no contact on the shooter's arm.

explanation.correct: A block is clean when the hand gets the ball and not the shooter. Good rim protectors change shots by being tall and timing it without contact.
explanation.incorrect: Contact with the ball only is legal. A foul would be contact on the shooter's arm or body, which is why rim protectors focus on timing and verticality.

payload.prompt: What is a good shot contest without fouling?

options.text: Getting a hand high in the shooter's line of sight, straight up, without hitting him.
Swiping down across the shooter's arm.
Standing still and watching the shot.

explanation.correct: A good contest gets there in time, hand high and straight up, so the shooter has to shoot over it. No contact means no foul, and a late hand can still bother the shot.
explanation.incorrect: Swiping down catches the arm, which is a foul, and standing still contests nothing. The clean contest is a hand straight up in the shooter's face.

payload.prompt: What is a shot block?

options.text: A defender knocks a shot attempt away cleanly, before it can score.
A foul called on a defender who hits the shooter.
Standing in front of a teammate to set a screen.

explanation.correct: A block is a clean swat of the ball after the shot is released. It counts as a stat, and it can send a message that the paint is closed.
explanation.incorrect: A foul on a shooter is not a block, and a screen is something the offense does. A block means the defender's hand gets the ball and stops the shot.

payload.prompt: Tap the area a rim protector patrols.

diagram.alt: Half-court diagram with the basket near the bottom edge. The painted lane rises above it, and a wing and the top of the arc are marked.

explanation.correct: A rim protector plays in and around the paint, close to the basket, where he can block or change shots at the rim and discourage drives.
explanation.incorrect: That spot is far from the basket. A rim protector anchors the defense in the paint, close enough to alter shots at the rim.

payload.question: What is she saying about their defense?

options.text: They have someone who blocks and changes shots near the basket.
They score well near the basket.
Their guards pressure the ball full court.
They never give up offensive rebounds.

payload.translation: She is praising the team's defense near the basket, especially shot-blocking and altering shots inside.

followUps.line: Yeah, nobody wants to drive on him.
followUps.why: It shows you get the effect: a good rim protector changes shots and scares drivers away.

followUps.line: Does that change their whole defense?
followUps.why: A good follow-up asking how the rim protector impacts the entire defensive scheme.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Rim protection is just good defense in the paint, especially blocking and altering shots.

lessons.title: Steals, pressure and traps
lessons.objective: Describe pressing, trapping and why gambling for steals is risky.

payload.prompt: What is a steal in basketball?

options.text: A defender takes the ball from an opponent, or intercepts a pass.
Taking a timeout when not allowed.
Scoring while the other team is not looking.

explanation.correct: A steal is when the defense gains the ball from the offense, by stripping it or picking off a pass. It is credited to the defender and usually starts a fast break.
explanation.incorrect: A steal is a defensive play, not a timeout or a sneaky score. It means taking the ball from the offense during play, and it counts as a stat.

payload.prompt: What is a full-court press?

options.text: Aggressive defense over the whole court, to force turnovers before the offense reaches half court.
Letting the offense cross half court and then packing the paint.
A defense that only guards the ball handler in the half court.

explanation.correct: A full-court press starts pressure right after the inbound pass, often with traps, to hurry the offense and force mistakes. Its risk is giving up easy baskets when it gets beaten.
explanation.incorrect: A press is the opposite of sitting back. The defense pressures the ball the entire length of the floor, hoping to force turnovers before the offense is set.

payload.prompt: Why is gambling for steals risky?

options.text: If the gamble misses, the defender is out of position and the offense gets an easy look.
Going for a steal is against the rules.
A steal attempt always stops the shot clock.

explanation.correct: A gambler leaves his man or his position to chase the ball. If he wins, it is a great play, but if he misses, the offense has a four-on-three advantage and an easy shot.
explanation.incorrect: Steal attempts are legal and do not stop the clock. The risk is tactical: a defender who misses has left his spot, so the offense has an open teammate.

payload.prompt: A ball handler is pinned near the sideline. Trap or stay home?

situation.narrative: A ball handler dribbles toward the sideline near half court. Two defenders are close, and the rest of the team is in position behind the ball.

facts.label: Risk
facts.value: A trap leaves one offensive player open

options.label: Trap the ball handler
options.consequence: The sideline cuts off his escape. He has to pick up his dribble or force a pass, and the rotating defenders can pick off a bad one or make him give it up.
considerations: The sideline acts as a third defender
Teammates behind the ball are ready to rotate
A skilled passer can still beat a trap

options.label: Stay with your assigned players
options.consequence: It is safer, since no offensive player is left open, but it gives up a good chance to force a turnover.
considerations: The sideline is a natural trap spot
Traps only work if the rotations behind them are ready

payload.expertNote: Sideline traps are classic because the boundary works as an extra defender. Coaches call them when the players behind the ball can rotate, since every trap leaves someone open.

payload.question: What is she calling for?

options.text: Two defenders should converge on the ball handler in the corner to force a turnover.
Guard him one-on-one and give him room.
Switch a bigger defender onto him.
Let him pass the ball out freely.

payload.translation: She is calling a defensive trap: two defenders should double-team the ball handler in the corner, which has limited escape routes.

followUps.why: You recognize that traps in tight spaces aim to create turnovers.

followUps.line: Someone has to cover the dump-out.
followUps.why: A good follow-up about rotation responsibility when a trap is set.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: A trap is just two defenders covering one ball handler. Corner traps are common because there is no escape.

lessons.title: Transition defense and the fast break
lessons.objective: Read numbers advantages and why getting back matters.

payload.prompt: What is transition defense?

options.text: Defending right after a change of possession, before the offense gets set.
Switching defenders on a screen.
Changing from man to zone.

explanation.correct: Transition defense is the scramble after a miss or turnover. The team that just lost the ball has seconds to sprint back, find a man and stop a quick score.
explanation.incorrect: Switching and zone changes are half-court choices. Transition defense is the hustle back right after the ball changes hands, before the offense is organized.

payload.prompt: What is a fast break?

options.text: A quick attack before the defense is set, often with more attackers than defenders.
A timeout called right after a steal.
A slow set play that uses the whole shot clock.

explanation.correct: A fast break attacks before the defense gets organized, often with a numbers edge like 3-on-2. The goal is an easy shot before the half-court game begins.
explanation.incorrect: A fast break is the opposite of a slow set play. The offense pushes the ball up the floor right after a steal or rebound to score before the defense is set.

payload.prompt: Three attackers run at a basket guarded by three defenders. Numbers advantage?

scene.alt: Three offensive players advance toward the basket while three defenders have already gotten back in front of them.

explanation.correct: Three on three is even, so there is no break advantage. A numbers advantage means more attackers than defenders, like 3-on-2, and that is what hustling back prevents.
explanation.incorrect: A numbers advantage needs more attackers than defenders. When the defense has matched the offense player for player, the break is even and the offense has to slow down and run a play.

payload.prompt: After a miss, a defender jogs back while the offense races past. Good transition defense?

scene.alt: A defender trots back toward his basket while two offensive players sprint ahead of him.

explanation.correct: Transition defense starts the instant possession changes. A jogging defender loses the race, and that is how teams end up giving up easy baskets.
explanation.incorrect: Good transition defense means sprinting back and finding a man before the offense arrives. Jogging leaves the defense outnumbered near the rim.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: Get back, they are in transition.

payload.question: What is she yelling?

options.text: Hurry back on defense, because the other team is racing up the floor.
Slow the game down and run a set play.
Switch every screen from here on.
Foul him before he can score.

payload.translation: She is warning that the other team is running a fast break. Her team needs to sprint back and find their men before an easy basket happens.

followUps.why: It shows you know a break is about numbers, and it is an easy question for her to answer.

followUps.line: Somebody has to cut them off at the rim.
followUps.why: A good follow-up about stopping the easy basket.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Transition just means the other team is attacking fast after a turnover or rebound. You do not need more than that to follow along.
